headline: Fake bomb emails empty hundreds of schools in Italy

sources.title: Bomb threat hoaxes prompt evacuation of Italian schools, alarm in UK and Ireland (CNN)
Schools across Italy evacuated after receiving email bomb alerts (Al Jazeera)
Schools in Italy, Ireland and UK evacuated after hoax bomb threats that also target Meloni (Euronews)
Schools evacuated across Italy after bomb threats (The Local)
Nuovo allarme bomba nelle scuole, inviate mail a centinaia di istituti in tutta Italia (Open)

chunks.text: On November 11, 2026, hundreds of schools across Italy had to [[evacuate]], or make everyone leave the building quickly. Someone {{sent out}} the same email to about 6,300 schools, Italy's [[education ministry]] said. The email claimed that a bomb was hidden in each school. Students {{filed out}} into streets and [[courtyards]]. In Rome, about 20 schools were affected, including [[elementary schools]] and a [[preschool]]. Parents were told to {{pick up}} their children.

verbs.correct: To send something to many people
verbs.wrong: To hide the name of a sender
verbs.why: Our school sends out a newsletter every Friday. The city sends out a warning before every big storm. Someone sent out the same email to about 6,300 schools in Italy on November 11, 2026.

verbs.correct: To leave one by one, in a line
verbs.why: Fans file out of the stadium after the game. The students file out of the hall when the bell rings. Students across Italy filed out into streets and courtyards.

verbs.correct: To go and get someone from a place
verbs.wrong: To ask someone to stay home
verbs.why: I pick up my son from soccer practice at six. Her dad picks her up after school every day. Parents in Rome were told to pick up their children from the schools.

chunks.text: The email was a [[hoax]], a false warning meant to scare people. Police {{went through}} the schools. The threats {{turned out}} to be fake. Italy's education minister said 312 schools were affected. He said the emails were most likely a [[cyberattack]], an attack made through computers, not a [[real threat]]. A teacher in Milan said some children [[cheered]] because they thought school had {{let out}} early.

verbs.wrong: To close a place for the day
verbs.why: Guards go through every bag at the stadium gate. The police go through a house carefully after a break-in. Police in Italy went through the schools after the bomb email.

verbs.correct: To be found to be something
verbs.wrong: To be sent to the wrong place
verbs.why: Some rumors turn out to be true. The weather often turns out better than the forecast says. The bomb threats at the Italian schools turned out to be fake.

verbs.correct: To end, so students can go home
verbs.why: School lets out at three o'clock. In June, our school lets out early on Fridays. A teacher in Milan said some children cheered because they thought school had let out early.

chunks.text: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the [[checks]] found no [[real danger]]. She said the emails seemed to be part of a plan to [[spread fear]]. Meloni {{sat down}} with the country's [[security chiefs]] for an [[emergency meeting]] the same day. She also invited [[opposition leaders]], the heads of parties outside the government, to talk on November 12. Investigators are trying to {{track down}} the sender. Italy's [[interior minister]], who is in charge of the police, said it was too early to say if the threats are [[connected]].

verbs.correct: To have a meeting to talk
verbs.wrong: To send a letter to someone
verbs.why: The coach sits down with each player after the season. Our manager sits down with new workers on their first day. Meloni sat down with Italy's security chiefs for an emergency meeting on November 11.

verbs.correct: To find someone or something after a search
verbs.wrong: To follow someone on social media
verbs.why: The police often track down stolen cars in a few days. Reporters track down people who saw the accident. Investigators in Italy are trying to track down the sender of the bomb emails.

chunks.text: Similar emails {{popped up}} at hundreds of schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Ireland the same day. Police there called them hoaxes and said most schools did not need to evacuate. It was not the first time in Italy. On November 2, another bomb email reached about 270 Italian schools, Italian media reported. In early November, [[fake bomb warnings]] also [[disrupted]] flights across Europe. Meloni did not {{rule out}} more emails like these.

verbs.wrong: To be blocked by a computer
verbs.why: Strange ads pop up on my screen all the time. New coffee shops pop up all over the city. Similar emails popped up at hundreds of schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Ireland.

verbs.correct: To say something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To call the police right away
verbs.why: The weather report rules out snow this weekend. The mayor does not rule out a new tax. Meloni did not rule out more emails like these in Italy.

mainIdea.s: A fake bomb email made hundreds of Italian schools send students outside on November 11. Police found no danger, and the government is trying to learn who sent the messages.
mainIdea.why: About 6,300 schools got the email, and hundreds evacuated. The threats turned out to be fake, and investigators are trying to track down the sender.

mainIdea.s: Thousands of schools in Italy got an email that warned of hidden bombs, so many emptied their buildings. Officials say a group of teenagers wrote it as a joke and were caught.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody has been caught. Investigators are still trying to track down the sender and learn if the threats are connected.

mainIdea.s: Italy's government plans to hire thousands of new teachers for public schools next year. The education minister says classes will get smaller and many towns will get new buildings.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a fake bomb email sent to about 6,300 Italian schools. Hundreds of schools evacuated, but the threats turned out to be fake.

tf.s: Someone sent out a fake bomb email to thousands of schools in Italy.
tf.why: The same email went to about 6,300 schools, and hundreds of them had to evacuate.

tf.s: Police found real bombs in several Italian schools.
tf.why: Police went through the schools and found no real danger. The threats were a hoax.

tf.s: The bomb threats against the Italian schools turned out to be fake.
tf.why: The email was a hoax. The education minister said it was most likely a cyberattack, not a real threat.

tf.s: Meloni sat down with security chiefs to talk about the threats.
tf.why: On the same day, the prime minister met with the country's security chiefs about the fake bomb emails.

tf.s: Investigators have caught the person who sent the bomb emails.
tf.why: Nobody has been caught. Investigators are still trying to track down the sender.

tf.s: No similar emails popped up at schools outside Italy.
tf.why: Similar emails popped up at hundreds of schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Ireland on the same day.

lines.text: Did you see the news from Italy? Hundreds of schools had to evacuate.
No, a bomb threat. Someone {{sent out}} the same email to about 6,300 schools.
[[Not again]]. Didn't that happen there on November 2, too?
It did, but this one was much bigger. Students {{filed out}} into the streets, and parents had to {{pick up}} their kids.
Well, [[safety first]]. Any principal would do the same.
Police {{went through}} the buildings, and the threats {{turned out}} to be fake.
Nobody. A teacher in Milan said some kids cheered because they thought school had {{let out}} early.
[[That's kids for you]]. A free day sounds great when you're ten.
So, [[no harm done]], but the government is worried. Meloni {{sat down}} with security chiefs the same day.
Good. They have to [[take it seriously]]. Do they know who sent it?
Not yet. Investigators are trying to {{track down}} the sender.
No. Similar emails {{popped up}} at schools in Scotland and Ireland, too.
Meloni didn't {{rule out}} more emails like these.
I hope they find the sender soon.

expressions.def: Used when something bad or annoying happens one more time
ex: The bus is late? Not again.
Not again! I forgot my lunch at home for the third time.

expressions.def: Used to say that staying safe is more important than anything else
ex: Wear your helmet when you ride. Safety first.

expressions.def: Used to say that this is how children usually act
ex: He ate the cake before dinner. That's kids for you.
They want to play in the rain. That's kids for you.

expressions.def: Used to say that nobody was hurt and nothing was damaged
ex: You spilled some water, but no harm done.
A ball hit the window, but the glass did not break, so no harm done.

expressions.def: To treat something as important and not as a joke
ex: The test is next week, so please take it seriously.
If your doctor gives you advice, take it seriously.
